newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin says Russian communists getting radical.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin says Russian communists getting radical.

text.p: A senior Kremlin aide said on Monday Russia's opposition communists were becoming more radical and sounded alarm bells over party calls to stage street protests and oust President Boris Yeltsin.

On the eve of what would have been Bolshevik revolutionary Vladimir Lenin's 127th birthday, Yeltsin aide Georgy Satarov hit back at a weekend Communist Party congress which urged activists to collect signatures ro demand the president's dismissal.
"The collection of signatures is an illegal act and it will have no legal consequences," Satarov, a Kremlin aide on relations with parliament and political parties, told Interfax news agency.
Satarov regarded the attack on Yeltsin as a sign of "a sharp radicalisation of the party", Interfax said.

The communists, worried by economic policies which they say are pushing Russia into chaos and a recent government reshuffle which promoted liberals, called for mass protests to mark the May 1 and May 9 public holidays.
Yeltsin, 66, and the communists are old foes. He won re-election last year partly by fanning fears of what he called a red tide sweeping back to power.

Despite their old rivalry, Yeltsin and the communists have stopped short on open confrontation since his re-election last July. The communists even approved Yeltsin's candidate, Viktor Chernomyrdin as prime minister, and passed this year's budget.

But the Kremlin has been upset by recent signs of hostility in parliament and appears to have been angered by the whistling and jeers which greeted a message of reconciliation which Yeltsin sent to the communists' congress.
One liberal television commentator, Yevgeny Kiselyov, said on Sunday the message could be Yeltsin's last olive branch to the most powerful opposition party.
"How will the president respond to this? I fear he has held out his hand to the communists for the last time," he said in his influential weekly current affairs programme Itogi.
Some independent politicians say a dangerous confrontation is not far away.

Others dismiss such fears, saying the communists are not interested in provoking Yeltsin into a battle or dissolving parliament because they fear losing the influence they have as the biggest party in the lower chamber, the State Duma.

Even though the communists called for Yeltsin to be ousted for health reasons during his almost eight-month absence with heart trouble last year and then pneumonia, their calls were never put to a vote in parliament.
Yeltsin's return had largely silenced the calls to oust him until the communists stepped up the pressure at the weekend.
Yeltsin has vowed to take on parliament if it picks a fight, evoking memories of how he used tanks to smash the old, hardline parliament into resistance in 1993.
Yeltsin spent Monday in the Black Sea resort of Sochi making the final preparations for a visit by Chinsese President Jiang Zemin, who arrives in Moscow on Tuesday.
Security officials were on the alert in southern Russia as separatists in Chechnya mourned the death a year ago of the breakaway region's late leader, Dzhokhar Dudayev.

Radical separatists threatened to mark the anniversary of his death in a rocket attack by attacking Russian cities. A bomb exploded near Chechnya, hurting no one, but officials said it was too soon to say if it was linked with Chechnya.
Russian officials said security had been tightened because of the threat of attacks, not because of any fears in unrest to commemorate Soviet state founder Lenin's birth in 1870.
